tldr: Fröhner and Sekar walk through four integration fundamentals (coupling dimensions, control flow, delivery semantics and ordering, noisy neighbours in shared queues) and the patterns and trade-offs for each.
summary: Dirk Fröhner and Sabarish Sekar, both AWS solutions architects, frame integration as part of the architecture rather than an afterthought, and cite the principle that every design option sucks in some way, so the job is to pick the one that sucks least. Starting from Larry Constantine's 'high cohesion, low coupling', Sekar breaks coupling into location, format, temporal and domain dimensions. A synchronous REST call from a booking service to a payment service carries all four, and they compound across call chains. Going asynchronous only removes waiting for processing; adding a queue also removes the availability dependency and buffers peaks. Domain coupling remains until you switch from commands to published events on a topic, where consumers choose to couple to the producer's 'ride booked' event. Topic-queue chaining (SNS into SQS) combines fan-out with buffering.

Fröhner separates data flow (what) from control flow (how): consumers pull from queues, which adds latency but enables load levelling. When producers outpace consumers, the two flow-control levers are TTL, dropping messages past a business-defined age, and producer back-pressure, both of which are business decisions. Sekar contrasts push (webhooks, EventBridge: routing, filtering, real-time) with pull (SQS: consumer-paced, simpler networking, windowed stream analytics).

On delivery, Sekar shows why exactly-once delivery is impossible, since a lost acknowledgement forces a retry, while exactly-once semantics can be had through deduplication bounded by scope or time (producer ID and sequence number in Kafka, a five-minute window in SQS), and consumers must still be idempotent. For ordering, Fröhner argues that partial order (per partition or message group) is enough for almost all business problems, and shows a consumer-side helper table that uses business versions to reorder and drop duplicates. The final pillar is noisy neighbours in a shared queue: per-tenant queues, cell-based sharding, shuffle sharding, hybrid dedicated queues, and dynamic producer- or consumer-triggered overflow queues, the last of which SQS fair queues implement.
keyPoints: Coupling is a spectrum across location, format, temporal (availability and waiting) and domain dimensions; reducing one can introduce another.

A queue removes the availability dependency and flattens peaks; a pub/sub topic reverses domain coupling so consumers couple to the producer's events. Use commands when the producer needs a result (payment), and events when it doesn't care (loyalty points).
Queue flow control has two levers: TTL (for example, drop booking requests older than a five-minute SLA) and producer back-pressure, which needs business context rather than a config switch.

Exactly-once delivery is impossible, but exactly-once semantics come from broker deduplication with limited scope (Kafka: producer ID plus sequence number; SQS: five-minute window), and consumers must still handle redeliveries.

Total order would need unbounded state; partial order via Kafka partitions or message groups suffices for most business cases, and a consumer helper table keyed on business versions can restore order and drop duplicates.

Cell-based sharding caps a noisy neighbour's blast radius at 1/cells (four cells = 25%, eight = 12.5%); shuffle sharding with two of eight queues gives 28 combinations, about 3.5% overlap, and about 0.02% with 100 shards.

Dynamic overflow queues can be triggered by producers that detect a spike or by consumers that see errors or slow processing; SQS fair queues provide the consumer-controlled variant if each message carries a tenant ID.
takeaways: For each integration, list which coupling dimensions it carries before choosing between REST, a queue or a topic.
Make every consumer idempotent and carry business IDs and version numbers in messages, regardless of what the broker promises.
Ask the business owner to set TTLs and back-pressure policy instead of treating them as purely technical settings.
If one shared queue serves many tenants, add a tenant ID to messages now and evaluate fair-queue or sharding options before a noisy neighbour appears.

quotes.text: All design options on the table that you have as an architect suck in a certain way, and your job is to identify the one that sucks less.
We cannot get exactly once delivery, but we can get exactly once semantics.
This is not a shortcoming of queues, quite the opposite. With the help of queues you make this visible.

watchIf: You design event-driven or queue-based systems and want a clear vocabulary for coupling, delivery guarantees, ordering and multi-tenant fairness.
